extracted.intended_audience: NIH communications staff, press officers, science communicators, and institutional public affairs professionals
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for drafting NIH press releases and public-facing communications about scientific research, emphasizing accuracy, transparency, plain language, and appropriate framing of clinical and public-health implications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scientific accuracy
rubrics_metrics.description: Scientific accuracy paramount / Scientific accuracy verified
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure all scientific claims, results, and interpretations are checked and verified; avoid exaggeration or misrepresentation of methods or findings. Cross-check facts with authors and subject-matter experts before publication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plain language
rubrics_metrics.description: Plain language for public understanding / Plain language for accessibility
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use nontechnical wording and clear explanations so lay audiences can understand significance and limitations. Avoid jargon; explain technical terms when necessary and keep sentences concise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methodology transparency
rubrics_metrics.description: Methodology transparency / Methodology summarized clearly / Methodology summarized
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Summarize study design and methods clearly in the release (and lede). Describe sample size, study type, and key procedures so readers can evaluate validity and relevance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations explicitly stated
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describe study limitations up front and honestly (e.g., sample size, generalizability, design constraints). Avoid burying limitations or omitting them altogether.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clinical relevance properly framed
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Place findings in proper clinical context — state whether results are preliminary, directly clinically actionable, or require further study. Avoid implying direct patient benefit when none is established.

rubrics_metrics.name: Translation to public health implications
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When possible, explain implications for public health while avoiding overstatement. Link findings to potential population-level impact only when evidence supports such claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Headline focus
rubrics_metrics.description: Focus on finding, not the institution
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write headlines that emphasize the scientific result or newsworthy finding rather than institutional names or promotions. Make the outcome the focus for reader interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Headline voice
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use active, direct phrasing in headlines to improve clarity and immediacy. Avoid passive constructions that dilute the message.

rubrics_metrics.name: Headline length
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep headlines concise to fit distribution channels and grab attention; aim for 80 characters or fewer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Headline caution language
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not use superlatives or claims of novelty (e.g., 'first', 'breakthrough') unless thoroughly verified and supported by the research and external validation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Headline newsworthiness
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Convey both the news element and why it matters; highlight significance and relevance to readers rather than only the factual result.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lede composition and length
rubrics_metrics.description: Finding, methodology summary, significance in 50 words
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Craft a lede of about 50 words that states the key finding, summarizes methodology, and explains significance succinctly to orient readers immediately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lede attribution details
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include names of principal investigators, institutions involved, and study dates in the lede or early paragraphs for transparency and attribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lede quantitative detail
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide concrete quantitative details (e.g., sample size, effect sizes) early so readers can assess the magnitude and robustness of findings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Background context
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give readers context about the condition, topic, or prior knowledge so the new findings can be placed within existing understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Body: detailed methodology
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In the body, expand on study design, methods, population, measures, analysis techniques, and other methodological details necessary for informed interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Body: specific findings with statistics
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report the principal results with statistical information (e.g., confidence intervals, p-values where appropriate) and absolute numbers to avoid misleading portrayals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Body: clinical relevance or lack thereof
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly state whether results have direct clinical application, are preliminary, or require more research before clinical translation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Body: future research directions
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mention next steps, open questions, or planned studies to clarify the trajectory of the research and avoid presenting findings as final.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quote: principal investigator
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include a substantive quote from the principal investigator that explains the work, its significance, and limitations in plain language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quote: NIH context
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include contextualizing quotes from an NIH official to situate the work within NIH priorities or broader public-health perspectives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quote: external expert
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When useful, add perspective from an independent external expert to corroborate significance, provide balance, or highlight limitations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quote: substantive scientific reasoning
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quotes should provide genuine scientific rationale or interpretation, not mere promotional statements; they should add explanatory value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quote: honesty about limitations
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure quoted remarks acknowledge limitations and avoid overstating findings; prioritize balanced, evidence-based language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish preclinical vs clinical
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clearly label whether the research is preclinical (e.g., lab, animal) or clinical (human subjects) to prevent misinterpretation of applicability to humans.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish animal vs human studies
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Always specify the species or human population studied and avoid implying human relevance when results are from animals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Risk communication: relative and absolute risks
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide both relative and absolute risks
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When reporting risk changes, include both relative and absolute measures so the practical magnitude is clear and not misleading.

rubrics_metrics.name: Funding disclosure
rubrics_metrics.guidance: List funding sources and sponsor information to identify potential influences and provide transparency about support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conflicts of interest disclosure
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disclose relevant financial or other conflicts of interest for investigators or institutions to allow readers to assess potential bias.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid causal claims for correlational findings
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not present correlation as causation; use cautious language (e.g., 'associated with' rather than 'causes') unless causal inference is justified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid 'cure' language for early-stage research
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid claiming cures or definitive solutions when findings are preliminary or preclinical; emphasize stage and remaining gaps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid hype exceeding the study
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refrain from sensationalizing results; match claims to the evidence and prioritize sober, accurate framing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid single-source claims on controversies
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid presenting contested findings as settled based on a single study; seek multiple expert perspectives or note ongoing debate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid effect sizes without baseline rates
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report effect sizes alongside baseline rates to give readers a sense of absolute change and real-world impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid equating statistical significance with clinical significance
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note when statistically significant findings may lack meaningful clinical impact; report both statistical and practical relevance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multimedia: researcher images with permission
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use photos of researchers when available and ensure permissions and credits are secured before publication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multimedia: visualizations of mechanisms
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include clear, accurate visuals explaining mechanisms when helpful; avoid misleading schematics and label graphics clearly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multimedia: patient stories with consent
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only use patient narratives or identifying information with documented consent and appropriate privacy protections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multimedia: charts showing results properly
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design charts that accurately reflect the data (proper axes, scales, error bars where appropriate) and avoid deceptive visualizations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multimedia: captions and credits
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide informative captions and attribute image/graphic sources and credits clearly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiple expert voices
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include perspectives from multiple experts (investigators, external experts, NIH officials) to provide balanced interpretation and validation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect sizes given fully
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report magnitude of effects in absolute terms and with measures of uncertainty so readers can judge importance and reliability.
